In the field of reinforcement learning, experience replay is a widely used technique that stores past experiences in a buffer and utilizes them to train policies. However, the standard approach to experience replay, which averages the losses from the buffer, has a significant drawback: it can lead to policy divergence when the buffer contains a wide range of experiences. This issue arises because the policy is optimized to minimize the expected loss, but the loss from the buffer is not expected due to its varying nature. To address this challenge, we propose a novel variance reduction approach that incorporates a new loss term into the policy optimization problem. This new term is derived from the buffer and is designed to minimize the variance of the loss, thereby reducing the policy divergence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on various tasks, including Atari games and robotic control, and show that it outperforms the standard experience replay method. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of our approach, which reveals that it is equivalent to a specific variant of the variance-reduced stochastic gradient descent algorithm. This connection enables us to leverage existing theoretical results to establish the convergence of our approach. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chenxunz/VRER.

The rapid growth of large language models has led to significant advancements in various NLP tasks, yet these models often struggle to generalize effectively across different tasks. This challenge is particularly pronounced when models are trained on a single task, as they frequently fail to adapt to new tasks without additional training data. To address this issue, we propose a novel unsupervised cross-task generalization framework that leverages a retrieval-based approach to augment the target task with relevant source task data. By utilizing a set of pre-trained task embeddings, our method efficiently retrieves the most relevant source task data for each target task sample, thereby enhancing the target task model's performance without requiring additional training data. We evaluate our approach on multiple cross-task generalization benchmarks, including the widely used CrossTask and Generalizing to Instructional Domains datasets, and achieve state-of-the-art results on both. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in real-world scenarios by applying it to a cross-domain sentiment analysis task. This approach is particularly beneficial for long-range dependencies and can be seamlessly integrated into existing attention-based neural machine translation architectures. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin. Moreover, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposed mechanism, including an examination of its impact on attention weights, model parameters, and training speed.
